1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [6:1](ta:06). This also occurs in verses 8 and 18.

2.note: See how you translated **Son of man** in [2:1](ta:02). This also occurs in verses 6, 9, 12, 14, 19, and 28.

Yahweh is using **set your face toward Jerusalem** as a common expression of the culture to mean “turn your attention toward Jerusalem in order to oppose it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [focus your attention on Jerusalem in order to oppose it]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if prophesying were making words **drivel**, that is, drip out like a liquid. It means that Ezekiel should let his message against **the sanctuaries** flow out continually. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and speak continually against the sanctuaries]

Ezekiel is speaking to the sanctuaries that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the coming judgment on the places where they worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sanctuaries. Alternate translation: [and speak out against the people who worship at the sanctuaries]

The implication is that **the sanctuaries** refers to the temple in Jerusalem and its holy places. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy places of the temple in Jerusalem]

Here, **the land of Israel** represents the people who live in the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

3.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֞ לְ⁠אַדְמַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הִנְ⁠נִ֣י אֵלַ֔יִ⁠ךְ
3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall say to the land of Israel that Yahweh says, ‘Look at me—against you]

Ezekiel is using a future statement to give an instruction or command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate the words **And you shall say to the land of Israel** using a command or instruction form. Alternate translation: [And say to the land of Israel]

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing **the land of Israel** as if it were a single person, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the expression **Look at me** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. The words **against you** mean that Yahweh is now the enemy of the land of Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen closely, I am now against you]

Here, **my sword** represents the army that Yahweh will send to attack the land of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verses 4 and 5. Alternate translation: [And I will send out my army to attack you]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if killing people were to **cut off** part of something. It means that Yahweh will kill the people who live in the land of Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 4. Alternate translation: [and I will kill among you righteous and wicked]

Yahweh is using the adjectives **righteous** and **wicked** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [righteous people and wicked people alike]

Yahweh is referring to all of the people in the land of Israel by naming two major groups: **righteous** and **wicked**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all people] or [everyone]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse.

The word translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [that is why]

Yahweh is using **all flesh** to represent all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against all people]
See how you translated this expression in 20:47.

5.note: The implication is that Yahweh will not put his sword back into its sheath until it has finished killing the people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [It will not return to its sheath until it has finished killing the people]

6.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [4:1](ta:04).

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [But, as for you, son of man]

The terms **groan with the breaking of loins** and **with bitterness, you shall groan** mean similar things. Ezekiel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [groan with deep anguish]

Groaning in great anguish where the people could see him was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed how greatly the people would grieve when they heard the news of the coming disaster. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [groan with the breaking of loins as a sign of how the people will mourn]
The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel who would be watching Ezekiel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the eyes of the Israelites]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Ezekiel’s great sorrow were a **breaking of loins**, that is, as if the middle part of his body were breaking. It means that Ezekiel should groan with such deep anguish that he seems to lose all of his strength. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with such deep anguish that you lose all your strength]

Here, **eyes** represents seeing. The phrase **to their eyes** means that Ezekiel should groan while the people are watching him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as the people of Israel look on]

7.q: יֹאמְר֣וּ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ עַל־מָ֖ה אַתָּ֣ה נֶאֱנָ֑ח וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֡ אֶל־שְׁמוּעָ֣ה
7.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [they will ask you why you are groaning. Then you shall answer them, ‘I am groaning because of a report]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel who see Ezekiel groaning. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites will say to you]

Ezekiel is using a future statement to give an instruction or command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words using a command or instruction form. Alternate translation: [Then say]

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I am groaning because of a report, for it is coming]

The implication is that the **report** is news about the disaster that Yahweh is about to bring on Jerusalem, and that **it** refers to that disaster. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Because of the news about the disaster that Yahweh is about to bring on Jerusalem, for that disaster is coming]

Here Ezekiel is speaking as if people’s courage were something in their **heart** that could **melt**. It means that everyone will lose courage and become very afraid. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And everyone will lose courage]

Here Ezekiel is speaking as if people’s loss of strength were their **hands** becoming loose and weak. It means that everyone will become too weak and afraid to do anything. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everyone will be too weak to do anything]

Here Ezekiel is speaking as if a person’s **spirit** were a light that could become **dim**. It means that everyone will become discouraged and lose hope. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everyone will lose hope]
See how you translated this expression in 7:17.

The expressions **It is coming** and **it will happen** mean similar things. Ezekiel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [It will surely come]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11. This also occurs in verse 13.

9.q: הִנָּבֵא֙ וְ⁠אָ֣מַרְתָּ֔ כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י אֱמֹ֕ר חֶ֥רֶב
9.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [prophesy and say that the Lord says that there is a sword]

Yahweh is repeating the word **sword** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [A terrible sword]

The expressions **sharpened** and **polished** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone has sharpened and also polished]

10.note: Here, **For the sake of** marks “slaughtering a slaughter” as the goal or purpose of “it has been sharpened.” In the same way, the second **for the sake of** marks “belonging to it lightning” as the goal or purpose of “it has been polished.” Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

The expressionS **it has been sharpened** and **it has been polished** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [someone has sharpened it… someone has polished it]

The meaning of the original language here is uncertain. However, it is likely that Ezekiel is using the question form to emphasize that the people have no reason to rejoice, because the sword is coming against them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We must not rejoice!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the royal authority of the king of Judah were a **scepter**, the rod that a king held as a sign of his authority. It means the royal power of the king of Judah, whom Yahweh calls **my son**, who himself represents the people of Judah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The royal power of the king of Judah]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the flash of the polished sword were **lightning**. It means that the sword has been polished so that it gleams and flashes brightly, the way lightning does. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [its flashing brilliantly]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if “The scepter of my son” were a person who could despise **every tree**, that is, every wooden rod. The meaning of the original language here is uncertain. This could mean: (1) that the royal power of Judah treats every other royal scepter as worthless, perhaps meaning that it refuses all correction or considers every other ruler to be inferior. (2) that the words of the original text here are difficult to understand and their meaning is not clear, in which case you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [considers itself superior to every other rod]

Here, **For the sake of** marks **slaughtering a slaughter** as the goal or purpose of **it has been sharpened**. In the same way, the second **for the sake of** marks **belonging to it lightning** as the goal or purpose of **it has been polished**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

The meaning of the original language here is uncertain. This could mean: (1) that Ezekiel is using the question form to emphasize that the people have no reason to rejoice, because the sword is coming against them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. (2) that the words of the original text here are difficult to understand and their meaning is not clear. In that case, you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [We must not rejoice!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the royal authority of the king of Judah were a **scepter**, the rod that a king held as a sign of his authority. It means the royal power of the king of Judah, whom Yahweh calls **my son**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The royal power of the king of Judah]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if **The scepter of my son** were a person who could despise **every tree**, that is, every wooden rod. The meaning of the original language here is uncertain. This could mean: (1) that the royal power of Judah treats every other rod as worthless, perhaps meaning that it refuses all correction or considers every other ruler to be inferior. (2) that the words of the original text here are difficult to understand and their meaning is not clear, in which case you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is considered superior to every other rod]

11.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the unnamed person who prepared the sword, probably the owner of the sword. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the one preparing the sword gave it to polish]

The expressions **has been sharpened** and **has been polished** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Someone has sharpened it, the sword; and someone has polished it]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. The phrase **to give it into the hand of a killer** means to give the sword to a soldier so that he can use it to kill people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that a killer can use it]

12.note: The terms **Cry out** and **wail** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Wail loudly]

12.q: כִּי הִיא֙ הָיתָ֣ה בְ⁠עַמִּ֔⁠י הִ֖יא בְּ⁠כָל נְשִׂיאֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
12.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for it is surely against my people, including all the leaders of Israel]

The expression **thrown** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was Yahweh. Alternate translation: [I am throwing them to the sword]

Yahweh is using **thrown to the sword, they are** as a common expression of the culture. This could mean: (1) that the leaders of Israel have been handed over to be killed by the sword along with Yahweh’s people. (2) that terrors caused by the sword have come upon the leaders of Israel along with Yahweh’s people. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are the ones given over to be killed by the sword]

Slapping the thigh was a symbolic action by which a person showed great grief and dismay. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [slap on the thigh to show great grief and dismay]

13.note: The expression **has been tested** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was Yahweh. Alternate translation: [For I have tested it]

13.q: וּ⁠מָ֕ה אִם גַּם שֵׁ֥בֶט מֹאֶ֖סֶת לֹ֣א יִֽהְיֶ֑ה
13.note: The meaning of the original language here is uncertain. This could mean: (1) that Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the royal power of Judah, which rejects correction, will certainly come to an end. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. (2) that the words of the original text here are difficult to understand and their meaning is not clear. In that case, you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And even the scepter that rejects correction will certainly come to an end!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the royal authority of the king of Judah were a **scepter**. It means the royal power of Judah, which is **rejecting** Yahweh’s correction. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the king of Judah who rejects correction]

14.note: Striking the palms of the hands together was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that Yahweh had decided to punish his people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. This also occurs in verse 17. Alternate translation: [and strike your palms together to show that Yahweh has decided to punish his people]

14.q: חֶ֣רֶב חֲלָלִ֔ים הִ֗יא חֶ֚רֶב חָלָ֣ל הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל
14.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **sword** that is characterized by the people whom it kills, **the slain**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [It is the sword that will kill people; it is the sword that will kill the great one]

Yahweh is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could surround people so that they cannot escape. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one that their enemies will use against them on every side]

The expression **be doubled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the sword strike twice—three times]

Yahweh is using **may the sword be doubled** as a common expression of the culture. This could mean: (1) that the sword should strike again and again. (2) that the sword should strike a second time and then a third time. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may the sword strike again and again]

15.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if people’s courage were something in their **heart** that could melt. It means that people will lose their courage and become very afraid. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people losing their courage]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the things that cause people to fall and die were **obstacles** over which people trip. This could mean: (1) that the sword will cause the ruin of many people. (2) that the sword will kill so many people that their dead bodies will lie on the ground like obstacles that cause others to stumble. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the multiplying of the things that cause people to fall and die]

Yahweh is using **gates** to represent the cities of Israel to which those gates belong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Against all their cities]

Here, **the point of a sword** represents soldiers armed with swords who attack the cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [armed soldiers ready to attack]

Yahweh is using **Ah**, a word that expresses a strong feeling of dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh no]

The expressions **is made** and **is withdrawn** are passive verbal forms. Here, **withdrawn** means pulled out of its sheath. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I have made it to flash like lightning; I have pulled it out of its sheath for slaughter]

16.note: Yahweh is speaking to the sword, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the destruction that the sword will cause. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sword. Alternate translation: [The sword will gather itself and go to the right! It will set itself and go to the left]

Yahweh is referring to all directions by naming two major components, **the right** and **the left**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Strike in every direction]

The expression **is appointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Wherever your edge points]

Here, **face** represents the edge of the sword, which faces in the direction that the sword strikes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Wherever your edge is directed]

17.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if his anger were **heat** that he could **settle**. It means that Yahweh will punish the people until his anger is satisfied. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will punish them until my anger is satisfied]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:15. This also occurs in verse 32.

19.q: שִׂים לְ⁠ךָ֣ שְׁנַ֣יִם דְּרָכִ֗ים לָ⁠בוֹא֙ חֶ֣רֶב מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל
19.note: Marking out two roads was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that the king of Babylon would come with his army to attack. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [set for yourself two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon to come, to show that the king of Babylon will come with his army to attack]

Here, **sword** represents the army of the king of Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the troops of the king of Babylon]

The implication is that **a hand** is a signpost, which may have been shaped like a hand, that points the way to a city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And create a signpost shaped like a hand pointing the way]

Here, **head** represents the beginning of something. The phrase **at the head of the way** refers to the place where the road to a city begins. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the beginning of the road that leads to]

20.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and another way you shall set for the sword to come to Judah, to fortified Jerusalem]

21.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the place where the road divides were the **mother** of the roads that come from it. It means that the king of Babylon stands at the fork in the road. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the fork in the road]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The phrase **shakes the arrows** refers to a kind of divination in which a person marked arrows with names or messages, shook them in a container, and then drew one out to learn what the gods wanted. If your readers would not be familiar with this practice, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [He draws lots using marked arrows]

The term **idols** here refers to a kind of small statue of a god that people kept in their homes and consulted for guidance. If your readers would not be familiar with what these idols are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [he inquires of the small household statues of gods]

The phrase **looks at the liver** refers to a kind of divination in which a person examined the liver of an animal that had been sacrificed in order to learn what the gods wanted. If your readers would not be familiar with this practice, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [he examines the liver of a sacrificed animal to learn the will of the gods]

22.note: Yahweh is using **On his right is the divination** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the divination that the king holds in his right hand tells him to attack Jerusalem.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The divination he holds in his right hand directs him to go to Jerusalem]

Yahweh is using **to open the mouth with murder** as a common expression of the culture. This could mean: (1) to shout the battle cry as the soldiers begin to kill. (2) to give the order to kill the people of the city. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to raise the war cry for the slaughter]

Yahweh is using **to lift up the voice with a shout** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to shout loudly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to shout loudly]
See how you translated the similar expressions in 4:2.
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:2.

23.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the people of Jerusalem]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **divination of emptiness** is a false omen that means nothing, so the people of Jerusalem think that the divination of the king of Babylon means nothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as meaningless as a false omen]

Yahweh is using **in their eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in their judgment” or “in their opinion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their opinion]

The implication is that the people of Jerusalem were trusting in **Sworn oaths**. This could mean: (1) that the people of Jerusalem had sworn oaths of loyalty to the king of Babylon, which they later broke. (2) that other people, such as their allies, had sworn oaths to help them, so they did not believe that the king of Babylon would defeat them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Sworn oaths of loyalty to Babylon’s king]

Yahweh is using **he is reminding of iniquity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is calling attention to their guilt so that they will be punished.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he is pointing out their guilt, which will cause them]

The expression **to be captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was the king of Babylon and his army. Alternate translation: [so that he and his army can capture them]

24.q: כֹּֽה אָמַר֮ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִה֒ יַ֗עַן הַזְכַּרְ⁠כֶם֙ עֲוֺ֣נְ⁠כֶ֔ם
24.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the Lord Yahweh says that because of remembering your iniquity]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s **rebellions** were things that had been hidden and were now being uncovered. It means that everyone can now clearly see how the people have rebelled. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as everyone sees how you have rebelled]

24.q: לְ⁠הֵֽרָאוֹת֙ חַטֹּ֣אותֵי⁠כֶ֔ם בְּ⁠כֹ֖ל עֲלִילֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם יַ֚עַן הִזָּ֣כֶרְ⁠כֶ֔ם בַּ⁠כַּ֖ף תִּתָּפֵֽשׂוּ
24.note: The expressions **are seen**, **being remembered**, and **will be seized** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who does these actions, it is clear from the context that everyone will see the people’s sins, Yahweh is the one who remembers them, and the king of Babylon and his army will seize them. Alternate translation: [so that everyone sees your sins in all your deeds—because I remember you, the king of Babylon and his army will seize you by the palm]

Here, **the palm** represents the power of the king of Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the power of the king of Babylon you will be seized]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4. This also occurs in verses 26 and 28.

25.q: וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ חָלָ֣ל רָשָׁ֔ע נְשִׂ֖יא יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אֲשֶׁר בָּ֣א יוֹמ֔⁠וֹ בְּ⁠עֵ֖ת עֲוֺ֥ן קֵֽץ
25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **profane wicked one, prince of Israel** with the information in the next verse about what the Lord Yahweh says to him. Alternate translation: [And the Lord Yahweh says this to you, profane wicked one, prince of Israel, whose day has come at the time of the iniquity of the end]

The implication is that the **profane wicked one, prince of Israel** is King Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [profane wicked one, prince of Israel, King Zedekiah]

Yahweh is using **who has come his day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “whose time to be punished has come.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whose time to be punished has arrived]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **time** that is characterized by **iniquity** that brings about the **end**, that is, the time when Yahweh will punish the prince’s iniquity once and for all. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. This also occurs in verse 29. Alternate translation: [at the time when your iniquity will be punished once and for all]

26.note: Here, **the turban** and **the crown** represent the royal authority of the king who wore them. Removing them represents taking away the authority of the prince of Israel to rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Take away his royal authority and remove him from being king]

The pronoun **This** refers to something that the context does not clearly identify. This could mean: (1) the way things are now, so that Yahweh means that nothing will remain as it now is. (2) the crown, so that Yahweh means that the crown will no longer belong to this man. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The way things are now will not remain as they are]

Yahweh is using the adjectives **low** and **high** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [Make high the people who are low, and make low the people who are high]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if a person’s importance were how **high** or **low** he is. It means that people who are unimportant will become important, and people who are important will become unimportant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make the unimportant important, and make the important unimportant]

27.note: Yahweh is repeating the word **ruin** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will make it a complete ruin]

The first **it** refers to the city of Jerusalem, which Yahweh will destroy, and the second **it** refers to the right to rule, which Yahweh will give to the one to whom it belongs. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will make the city … and I will give him the right to rule]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one to whom it rightfully belongs]

The implication is that the person to whom **the judgment** belongs is someone who has the right to rule as king. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one who has the authority to rule as king]

28.q: הִנָּבֵ֤א וְ⁠אָֽמַרְתָּ֙ כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהֹוִ֔ה אֶל בְּנֵ֥י עַמּ֖וֹן וְ⁠אֶל חֶרְפָּתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֗ חֶ֣רֶב חֶ֤רֶב
28.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [prophesy, and you shall say what the Lord Yahweh says concerning the sons of Ammon and concerning their reproach. And you shall say that there is a sword, a sword]

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. This could mean: (1) the insults that the people of Ammon spoke against Israel. (2) the disgrace that the people of Ammon will suffer when Yahweh punishes them. Alternate translation: [and concerning how they insulted Israel]

28.q: חֶ֣רֶב חֶ֤רֶב פְּתוּחָה֙ לְ⁠טֶ֣בַח מְרוּטָ֔ה לְ⁠הָכִ֖יל
28.note: The expressions **opened** and **polished** are passive verbal forms. Here, **opened** means drawn out of its sheath. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A sword, a sword that the enemy has drawn for slaughter and has polished to consume]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the sword were an animal that could **consume** its prey. It means that the sword will destroy people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [polished to destroy people]

29.q: בַּ⁠חֲז֥וֹת לָ⁠ךְ֙ שָׁ֔וְא בִּ⁠קְסָם לָ֖⁠ךְ כָּזָ֑ב
29.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the prophets and diviners of the people of Ammon, who gave them false messages. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when your prophets envision emptiness of you, when your diviners divine a lie of you]

29.q: לָ⁠תֵ֣ת אוֹתָ֗⁠ךְ אֶֽל צַוְּארֵי֙ חַֽלְלֵ֣י רְשָׁעִ֔ים
29.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if killing people were putting a sword **on the necks** of people. It means that the sword will kill these wicked people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to use you to kill the profane wicked]

Yahweh is using the adjectives **profane wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with an equivalent phrase. This also occurs in verse 25. Alternate translation: [the profane wicked people]

30.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Return the sword to its sheath!]

The expressions **In the place where you were created** and **in the land of your origins** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [In the very land where you came from]

The expression **were created** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was Yahweh. Alternate translation: [In the place where I created you]
The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Ammon as a single nation, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

31.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **indignation** were a liquid that he could **pour** on people. It means that Yahweh will punish the people of Ammon severely because he is very angry with them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will punish you severely because I am very angry with you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **wrath** were a **fire** and as if he would **blow** that fire against the people of Ammon. It means that he will punish them severely because he is extremely angry with them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Because I am furious with you, I will punish you severely]

Here, **hand** represents power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will put you under the control of brutish men]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the men who will destroy the people of Ammon were **craftsmen**, people who are skilled at making things. It means that these men are experts at destroying people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [men who are skilled at destroying]

32.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if being burned up were being eaten as **food** by **the fire**. It means that the people of Ammon will be completely destroyed by fire. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The fire will completely burn you up]

Here, **Your blood** represents a violent death. The phrase **will be in the midst of the land** means that the people of Ammon will be killed in their own land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You will be killed violently in your own land]

The expression **will not be remembered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, you could say that no one will remember them. Alternate translation: [People will not remember you]
